tool.name: Grafana
tool.tagline: Dashboards, exploration and alerting on top of your metrics, logs and traces
tool.description: Grafana is an open-source observability front end: it queries data sources such as Prometheus, Loki, PostgreSQL or cloud monitoring services and shows the results as interactive dashboards. Teams use it to watch systems in real time, investigate incidents with logs and traces side by side, and alert on what they see. It is the most common way to visualize Prometheus metrics.

modules.name: Logs, traces and other data sources

concepts.name: What Grafana is
concepts.summary: Grafana queries many data sources and visualizes them in dashboards; it stores almost no monitoring data itself.
concepts.why: Knowing that Grafana is a query-and-display layer explains where data, performance and permissions really live.
concepts.body:
**Grafana** is a web application for visualizing and alerting on data that lives **elsewhere**. It connects to **data sources** such as Prometheus, Loki (logs), Tempo (traces), Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, MySQL, InfluxDB, CloudWatch or Azure Monitor, sends them queries and draws the results.

The main concepts:

- **Data source**: a configured connection with a URL and credentials.
- **Dashboard**: a page of **panels** arranged in a grid, with a shared time range and **variables** (drop-downs) at the top.
- **Panel**: one or more queries plus a **visualization** such as a time series graph, stat, gauge, table, heatmap or logs view.
- **Explore**: an ad-hoc query view for investigations, without building a dashboard.
- **Alerting**: rules that evaluate queries and notify through contact points.

Grafana itself stores only its own configuration (dashboards, users, alert rules) in a database, SQLite by default. Your metrics stay in Prometheus, so a slow panel is usually a slow query in the data source.

Grafana is open source (AGPLv3). Grafana Cloud offers it as a hosted service together with Prometheus-compatible storage (Mimir), Loki and Tempo, and Grafana Enterprise adds features like fine-grained access control and reporting.
takeaways: Grafana queries data sources and visualizes results; it doesn't store metrics
Dashboards contain panels; panels contain queries and a visualization
Explore is for ad-hoc investigation

quiz.q: A Grafana panel showing Prometheus data loads slowly. Where is the cause most likely?
options: The PromQL query being evaluated by Prometheus
quiz.explain: Grafana only forwards queries; heavy queries are evaluated by the data source.

concepts.name: Installing Grafana and adding Prometheus
concepts.summary: Run Grafana in Docker, log in, and connect a Prometheus data source with the right URL and scrape interval.
concepts.why: Nothing appears in Grafana until a data source is connected correctly, and the URL is the most common mistake.
concepts.body:
Grafana runs as a single server process, from OS packages, a binary or the official Docker image `grafana/grafana`. It listens on port **3000**; the first login is `admin` / `admin`, and you're asked to change the password immediately. Configuration lives in `grafana.ini` (or `custom.ini`), and any setting can be overridden by environment variables named `GF_<SECTION>_<KEY>`, such as `GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Data such as the SQLite database and plugins live in `/var/lib/grafana`; mount a volume there.

Add a data source under **Connections, Data sources, Add new data source, Prometheus**:

- **URL**: the address as seen **from the Grafana server**, not from your browser. In Docker Compose that is the service name, such as `http://prometheus:9090`; `localhost` there means the Grafana container itself.
- **Scrape interval**: set it to your Prometheus scrape interval (e.g. 15s). Grafana uses it to compute safe `rate()` ranges.
- Authentication if Prometheus is behind a proxy.

**Save & test** runs a test query. Queries are sent by the Grafana backend (server-side), so Prometheus doesn't need to be reachable from users' browsers.
concepts.code:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.13.4
    ports: ["9090:9090"]
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:13.2.0
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: change-me      # instead of admin/admin
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
volumes:
  grafana-data: {}
# In Grafana: Connections > Data sources > Prometheus
#   URL: http://prometheus:9090    (service name, not localhost)
#   Scrape interval: 15s
# Save & test -> "Successfully queried the Prometheus API."
takeaways: Grafana listens on :3000; settings via grafana.ini or GF_ environment variables
Data source URLs are resolved from the Grafana server
Set the data source scrape interval to match Prometheus
pitfalls: Using http://localhost:9090 when Grafana runs in a container; it points at the Grafana container.

quiz.q: Grafana runs in Docker Compose next to a service named prometheus. Which data source URL works?
quiz.explain: Inside the Compose network, containers reach each other by service name.

concepts.name: Your first dashboard and panels
concepts.summary: Create a dashboard, add time series and stat panels with PromQL queries, set legends and the time range, and save it.
concepts.why: Dashboards are what most people use Grafana for, and a few good habits make them readable from day one.
concepts.body:
Create a dashboard with **Dashboards, New, New dashboard, Add visualization**, and pick the data source. The panel editor has three areas: the preview, the **query** section below it, and the **visualization options** on the right.

For Prometheus the query editor has a **Builder** mode (pick metric, labels and operations) and a **Code** mode for typing PromQL. Useful query options:

- **Legend**: `{{instance}}` or `{{status}}` to name series by label instead of the full label set.
- **Min step / interval** and **Type** (range, instant, both). Stat and table panels often need **instant** queries.

Common visualizations: **Time series** for trends, **Stat** for one big number with a sparkline, **Gauge** and **Bar gauge** for values against limits, **Table** for lists, **Heatmap** for histogram distributions.

The dashboard's **time picker** (top right) sets the range for every panel, such as "Last 6 hours", plus an auto-refresh interval. Drag panels to arrange them and group them in collapsible **rows**.

Save the dashboard into a **folder** with a meaningful name. Each save creates a version you can compare and restore under **Settings, Versions**. Start with a few signals that answer "is the service healthy?" (traffic, errors, latency) rather than every metric you have.
concepts.code:
# Panel 1: Time series "Requests per second", legend {{status}}
sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))

# Panel 2: Stat "Error ratio", unit Percent (0.0-1.0), instant query
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

# Panel 3: Time series "p95 latency", unit seconds
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Panel 4: Stat "Targets up", instant query
sum(up{job="api"})
takeaways: Panels = query + visualization + options
Use legend templates like {{status}} and instant queries for stats
Save into folders; every save is a restorable version
pitfalls: One dashboard with 60 panels of every metric; nobody can read it during an incident.

quiz.q: Which visualization best shows the current error ratio as one large number?
quiz.explain: Stat displays a single reduced value, optionally with a sparkline and colour thresholds.

concepts.name: Time range, zoom and auto-refresh
concepts.summary: Use the time picker's relative and absolute ranges, zoom into graphs, share links with the range, and set auto-refresh sensibly.
concepts.why: Every panel on a dashboard is driven by the time range; knowing how to move around in time is the basic investigation skill.
concepts.body:
The **time picker** (top right) sets one time range for the whole dashboard. Ranges are written in Grafana's relative syntax: `now-6h` to `now` is the last six hours, `now/d` rounds to the start of today, and `now-1d/d` to `now-1d/d` is all of yesterday. You can also type absolute timestamps or pick them on a calendar. The dashboard's **timezone** (browser, UTC or a named zone) is set in the picker and stored with the dashboard.

Moving around:

- **Drag** across a time series panel to zoom into that span; the whole dashboard follows.
- The **zoom out** button (or `t` then `z`) doubles the range; the arrows (`t` then left or right) shift the window.
- The range is part of the URL as `from=now-6h&to=now` or epoch milliseconds, so a copied link reproduces exactly what you see. The **Share** menu can lock the link to absolute time.

The **refresh picker** next to it re-runs all queries every 5s, 10s, 30s, 1m and so on. The allowed list and a server-wide floor (`min_refresh_interval` in `grafana.ini`) are configurable; a wall-screen dashboard refreshing every 5 seconds is a real load on the data source.

In **Dashboard settings** you can hide the picker, set a **now delay** (shift "now" back by, say, 1m so the last, still-incomplete data point isn't drawn as a drop), and save the current range as the dashboard default. A single panel can deviate from the dashboard with **relative time** and **time shift** in its query options, for example "last 24h, shifted 7d" to show the same panel one week earlier.
concepts.code:
# Relative range syntax (from -> to)
# now-6h      now        last 6 hours
# now-7d      now        last 7 days
# now/d       now/d      today (00:00 to 23:59:59)
# now-1d/d    now-1d/d   yesterday
# now/w       now        this week so far
# now-1M/M    now-1M/M   previous calendar month

# The range travels in the URL:
# https://grafana.example.com/d/abc123/api?from=now-6h&to=now&timezone=utc
# https://grafana.example.com/d/abc123/api?from=1760680800000&to=1760702400000

# grafana.ini: no dashboard may refresh faster than every 10s
[dashboards]
min_refresh_interval = 10s
takeaways: now-6h, now/d and now-1d/d are the relative range syntax
Drag on a graph to zoom; the range is in the URL so links reproduce the view
Auto-refresh is load on the data source; set a now delay to hide the incomplete last point
pitfalls: Sharing a link with from=now-1h during an incident; by the time someone opens it the interesting hour has scrolled away.

quiz.q: Which range shows all of yesterday, from midnight to midnight?
quiz.explain: /d rounds to day boundaries; now-1d/d as both ends is the whole previous day.

concepts.name: Explore: ad-hoc queries and split view
concepts.summary: Use Explore to try PromQL without a dashboard: the metrics browser, Builder and Code modes, split view, query history and "Add to dashboard".
concepts.why: Most queries start as an experiment; Explore is where you find the right expression before it earns a place on a dashboard.
concepts.body:
**Explore** (the compass icon) is a scratchpad: choose a data source, write a query, run it and see a graph plus a table of the raw series, with no dashboard to save. It has the same time picker and the same query editor as the panel editor.

For Prometheus:

- **Metrics browser** (in Code mode) lists metric names and, after you pick one, its label names and values, so you can discover what is actually scraped before writing anything.
- **Builder** mode composes a query from a metric, label filters and operations such as rate and sum by; **Code** mode is plain PromQL with autocompletion and an **Explain** toggle that describes each step.
- **Options** below the query: range or instant type, legend, min step, and **Format** (time series, table, heatmap).

**Split view** opens a second Explore pane next to the first, with its own data source, sharing the time range by default (the link icon unlinks them). The classic use is metrics on the left and the matching Loki logs on the right. Each pane's state is encoded in the URL, so Explore links are shareable.

**Query history** keeps everything you ran, lets you star useful queries and add comments; **Query inspector** shows the exact request, the response and timing. When a query is right, **Add to dashboard** creates a panel in a new or existing dashboard.

Viewers can use Explore only if their role allows it; on busy production instances admins sometimes restrict it because an unbounded `{__name__=~".+"}` query hurts the data source.
concepts.code:
# A typical Explore session, Prometheus data source, Code mode

# 1. Discover: what does the api job expose? (metrics browser, or:)
{job="api"}                              # instant query, lists every series

# 2. Narrow down
rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])

# 3. Shape it, check the legend
sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))

# 4. Split view: right pane -> Loki, same time range
{app="api"} |= "error"

# 5. Add to dashboard -> panel in "API overview"
takeaways: Explore runs queries without a dashboard; Builder, Code and the metrics browser help find them
Split view puts two data sources side by side on one time range
Query history and Add to dashboard turn experiments into panels
pitfalls: Running an unfiltered selector over a large range in Explore and taking Prometheus down with you.

quiz.q: You want to see error logs next to a request-rate graph for the same time range. What do you use?
options: Explore split view with Prometheus on one side and Loki on the other
Two browser windows with separate time pickers
quiz.explain: Split view shows two panes with different data sources and a linked time range.

concepts.name: Time series panel, legend and tooltips
concepts.summary: Configure the time series visualization: lines, bars, points, fill and stacking, axes, null handling, legend modes with calculations, and tooltip modes.
concepts.why: Time series is the default visualization and the one you will tune most; its options decide whether a graph is readable at a glance.
concepts.body:
The **Time series** visualization draws every series the query returns against time. Its main option groups:

- **Graph styles**: lines, bars or points; line width and interpolation (linear, smooth, step before/after, the right choice for counters that change in steps); **fill opacity** and gradient; **show points** auto/always/never.
- **Stack series**: off, normal or 100%. Stacking only makes sense when the series add up to a meaningful total, like requests by status; never stack latencies.
- **Connect null values** and **Disconnect values**: by default a gap in data is drawn as a gap, which is usually what you want, since it reveals missing scrapes.
- **Axis**: placement left/right, soft min and max (axis grows beyond them if data does), log scale, and centered zero. Overrides let one series use the right axis, for example a request count next to a latency.
- **Thresholds** can be drawn as lines or filled regions, which gives a visual SLO line.

The **legend** has a mode (list, table, hidden), a placement (bottom, right) and **values**: calculations such as Last, Max, Mean and Total appended per series, sortable in table mode. Clicking a series name isolates it; Ctrl/Cmd-click adds more. Legend templates such as `{{instance}}` (set on the query) decide the names.

**Tooltip** mode is single, all or hidden; in all mode you can sort by value, which is handy with many series. The dashboard-level **Graph tooltip** setting (Settings, General) switches on a shared crosshair or shared tooltip across every panel, so hovering one graph marks the same moment on all of them.
takeaways: Stack only series that add up; keep gaps for missing data
Legend table mode with Last/Max/Mean turns a graph into a summary
Shared crosshair aligns hover across all panels
pitfalls: Switching on Connect null values everywhere, which hides scrape gaps and outages as smooth lines.

quiz.q: Which series are safe to stack in a time series panel?
options: Requests per second split by status code
CPU usage of two unrelated clusters as percentages
Any series, stacking is purely cosmetic
quiz.explain: Stacking shows parts of a whole; status-code request rates sum to total traffic, latencies and percentages don't.

concepts.name: Units, thresholds, value mappings and overrides
concepts.summary: Make panels readable with units, decimals, min and max, colour thresholds, value mappings and per-series overrides.
concepts.why: A correctly labelled number with a clear colour beats a raw float that everyone has to interpret.
concepts.body:
Panel options on the right of the editor fall into two kinds.

**Panel options** (title, description, links) and visualization-specific settings such as line width, stacking or the stat's colour mode.

**Field options**, which apply to the data values:

- **Unit**: seconds, bytes (IEC or SI), percent (0-100) or percent (0.0-1.0), requests per second and many more. Grafana then scales values automatically: 0.25 s shows as 250 ms, 1536 bytes as 1.50 KiB.
- **Min / Max** and **Decimals**.
- **Thresholds**: base colour plus steps, such as green, yellow above 0.01, red above 0.05. Gauges and stats colour themselves; time series can show threshold lines or areas.
- **Value mappings**: turn values into text, like `1` into "UP" and `0` into "DOWN", or ranges into labels.
- **Data links**: clickable URLs built from values and labels, for example to a logs query or another dashboard.

**Overrides** change field options for specific series only: by name, regex, query or field type. Typical uses are a different unit for one series, a dashed line for "last week", or a fixed colour for errors.

Set units in Grafana rather than multiplying in PromQL, so values stay correct and readable at every scale.
takeaways: Set the unit and let Grafana scale values
Thresholds colour values; mappings turn values into text
Overrides change options for selected series only
pitfalls: Choosing percent (0-100) for a ratio between 0 and 1, so 5% shows as 0.05%.

quiz.q: Your query returns 0.0312 for a ratio. Which unit shows it as 3.12%?
quiz.explain: Percent (0.0-1.0), called percentunit in JSON, multiplies the ratio by 100 for display.

concepts.name: Stat, gauge and bar gauge
concepts.summary: Show single values well: the reduce calculation, colour and graph modes of Stat, min/max and markers for Gauge, and Bar gauge for comparing many values.
concepts.why: The big numbers at the top of a dashboard are what people read first, and a wrong reduce calculation makes them lie.
concepts.body:
All three visualizations reduce each series to **one value** and colour it with the thresholds from field options.

**Value options** apply to all of them. **Calculation** picks how a series becomes one number: `Last *` (last value, even if null), `Last` non-null, Mean, Max, Min, Total, Count, Difference, and more. For a range query showing "current error ratio" you want Last non-null; for "requests in the selected range" you want Total of an `increase()`, or better an instant query over `$__range`. With an **instant** query there is only one value and the calculation doesn't matter. **Fields** chooses which numeric fields are shown, and **Limit** caps how many series are displayed.

**Stat** shows the number, optionally with a **sparkline** (graph mode area) and a name. Colour mode is none, value, background gradient or background solid; text mode is auto, value, value and name, or name. Orientation and text size tune layouts with many instances; one stat per `$instance` with repeat is common. Newer versions can show a **percent change** against the first value of the range.

**Gauge** needs a meaningful **min** and **max** (set them explicitly, otherwise Grafana guesses from the data) and shows threshold markers and labels around the arc. Use it for things with a natural limit: disk, memory, queue capacity.

**Bar gauge** draws one horizontal or vertical bar per series, in gradient, retro LCD or basic display mode, with sorting and a shared max. It is the right choice for "top 10 pods by memory" or the fill level of many disks.
concepts.code:
# Stat: Error ratio (instant query, unit percentunit, thresholds green/orange 0.01/red 0.05)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

# Stat: Requests in selected range (instant, calculation irrelevant)
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__range]))

# Gauge: Disk used, unit percentunit, min 0, max 1
1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"}

# Bar gauge: Memory by pod, unit bytes, sort descending, instant
topk(10, sum by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="prod"}))
takeaways: Stat, gauge and bar gauge reduce each series with a calculation; pick Last non-null or use instant queries
Gauges need explicit min and max
Bar gauge compares many series on one scale
pitfalls: Leaving the calculation at Mean for a "current value" stat, so it shows the average of the last 6 hours.

quiz.q: A Stat panel uses a range query and should show the current value. Which calculation is right?
quiz.explain: Last non-null takes the newest real sample; Mean and Total summarise the whole range.

concepts.name: Table panel
concepts.summary: Build readable tables: instant queries in table format, column filters, cell display modes (coloured background, gauge, sparkline) and footers.
concepts.why: Lists of instances, pods, endpoints or customers are tables, and a table needs its data in a different shape than a graph does.
concepts.body:
A **Table** shows data frames as rows and columns. The first thing to get right is the **shape** of the data. A Prometheus range query gives one frame per series with a time column, which the table shows as separate frames with a selector; what you usually want is one row per series, so set the query **Type** to **instant** and **Format** to **Table**. Each label becomes a column, plus `Time` and `Value`. For several queries, the Merge transformation combines them into one table, and Organize fields renames and hides columns.

Useful options:

- **Column filter** adds a filter control per column; **pagination** and a **footer** with calculations (Total, Mean, Count) help long tables.
- **Column width**, **minimum width** and **cell height**; **align** left, center or right.
- **Cell options**, set per column with overrides: coloured text or **coloured background** driven by thresholds, a **gauge** inside the cell, **sparkline** (needs the Time series to table transformation), JSON view for nested objects, image, or an **Actions**/data link cell.
- Value mappings turn `0`/`1` into "down"/"up" with colours, which reads far better than numbers.

Sorting is by clicking a header, or permanently with the Sort by transformation. Hide the `Time` column of instant queries; it only holds the evaluation time.

Tables render everything the query returned, so keep result sets small with `topk()` or SQL `LIMIT`; thousands of rows make the browser crawl and nobody reads them anyway.
takeaways: Instant query + Table format gives one row per series
Cell options (coloured background, gauge, sparkline) are set per column with overrides
Keep tables short with topk() or LIMIT
pitfalls: Using a range query in a table and getting a frame picker with hundreds of timestamps per series.

quiz.q: A Prometheus table shows a drop-down of frames instead of one row per instance. What fixes it?
options: Set the query to instant and format Table
quiz.explain: Range queries return a time series per instance; an instant query in table format yields one row each.

concepts.name: Heatmap, state timeline and logs panels
concepts.summary: Draw latency distributions from Prometheus histograms as heatmaps, show discrete states over time with state timeline and status history, and embed logs.
concepts.why: Averages hide the shape of latency and up/down states; these visualizations show distribution and state changes that a line graph can't.
concepts.body:
**Heatmap** shows how a distribution changes over time: the X axis is time, the Y axis the value buckets, and colour the count in each cell. For a Prometheus **histogram**, query the `_bucket` series summed by `le` and set the query **Format** to **Heatmap**: Grafana then sorts the buckets, converts cumulative counts into per-bucket counts and labels the Y axis with the bucket bounds. Native histograms are supported directly. Options cover the colour scheme and scale (exponential works well for latency), Y axis unit, bucket count for raw data, and **Calculate from data**, which bins plain time series yourself when the source has no buckets. Exemplars appear as dots on the heatmap.

**State timeline** shows discrete values per series as coloured bars along time: service up or down, deployment phase, feature flag state, alert state. Feed it values and give them meaning with **value mappings** (1 to "up" in green, 0 to "down" in red) or thresholds; **Merge equal consecutive values** collapses runs into one bar. **Status history** is the same idea on a periodic grid, one cell per interval, nicer for many series over long ranges.

The **Logs** visualization embeds a Loki (or Elasticsearch) query on a dashboard, with options to show time, wrap lines, prettify JSON, deduplicate and order. Keep the query narrow and pair it with the dashboard variables so logs follow the selected service.

Together with time series these cover most needs; the Grafana catalogue also has Candlestick, Node graph, Geomap, Canvas and Flame graph for specialised data.
concepts.code:
# Heatmap panel: request latency distribution
# Query options -> Format: Heatmap, Type: range
sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Y axis unit: seconds; colour scale: exponential

# State timeline: target health, value mappings 1 -> UP (green), 0 -> DOWN (red)
# Legend: {{instance}}
max by (instance) (up{job="api"})

# Status history: did the nightly job succeed each day? (0 = failed, 1 = ok)
max_over_time(job_last_run_success{job="etl"}[1d])

# Logs panel (Loki) following the dashboard variable
{app="$service", env="$env"} | json | level="error"
takeaways: Histogram buckets summed by le + Format: Heatmap = latency distribution over time
State timeline needs value mappings to turn numbers into named, coloured states
Logs panel embeds a narrow Loki query that follows the dashboard variables
pitfalls: Forgetting to sum by le, so every instance contributes its own set of buckets and the heatmap is noise.

quiz.q: What must a Prometheus query for a heatmap panel do?
options: Sum the _bucket series by le and use the Heatmap format
quiz.explain: Grafana needs one series per bucket bound (le) to build the Y axis and compute per-bucket counts.

concepts.name: Dashboard variables and templating
concepts.summary: Add drop-down variables from label values, use them in queries with multi-value and All options, and repeat panels per value.
concepts.why: One templated dashboard replaces a copy per service, environment or instance.
concepts.body:
**Variables** appear as drop-downs at the top of a dashboard and are referenced in queries as `$name` (or `${name}`). Create them under **Settings, Variables**. Types include:

- **Query**: values from the data source. For Prometheus: `label_values(up, job)`, `label_values(http_requests_total{job="$job"}, instance)` (variables can depend on each other), or `query_result(...)` for computed lists.
- **Custom**: a fixed comma-separated list.
- **Data source**: switch between, say, several Prometheus servers.
- **Interval**, **Constant** and **Text box**.

With **Multi-value** or **Include All** enabled, a variable can hold several values. Grafana formats them for the data source; in PromQL use the regex matcher: `{job=~"$job"}`. A custom **All value** like `.*` avoids huge regexes when there are many values.

Built-in variables are always available: `$__interval` and `$__rate_interval` (based on the time range and panel width), `$__range` (the dashboard range, e.g. for `increase(x[$__range])`), and `$__dashboard`, `$__user`.

**Repeat** options create one panel, or one row, per selected value: choose the variable in the panel's **Repeat options**. Variable selections are stored in the URL (`?var-job=api`), so links share the exact view.
concepts.code:
# Variable "job"      (Query, Prometheus)
label_values(up, job)
# Variable "instance" (Query, Multi-value, Include All, depends on $job)
label_values(up{job="$job"}, instance)

# Panel query using both; =~ because instance may hold several values
sum by (instance) (
  rate(http_requests_total{job="$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))

# Requests during the whole selected time range (Stat panel)
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="$job"}[$__range]))

# Shareable link with selections:
# /d/abc123/api?var-job=api&var-instance=All&from=now-6h&to=now
takeaways: label_values(metric, label) fills drop-downs from Prometheus
Use =~ with multi-value and All variables
$__rate_interval and $__range are built-in variables
pitfalls: Using job="$job" with a multi-value variable; it needs =~ to match several values.

quiz.q: A multi-value variable $env has prod and staging selected. Which matcher works?
quiz.explain: Grafana renders multiple values as a regex alternation, which needs the =~ matcher.

concepts.name: Transformations
concepts.summary: Reshape query results inside Grafana: join and merge queries, reduce series to rows, rename, filter and calculate fields.
concepts.why: Tables and comparisons often need data shaped differently than the data source returns it.
concepts.body:
**Transformations** (the Transform tab of the panel editor) process query results **after** they return and before visualization. They are applied in order, and you can inspect each step's output with the debug view.

Frequently used ones:

- **Merge**: combine several queries into one table, matching on common fields such as time and labels. The usual way to build a table with one column per query.
- **Join by field**: join frames on a field, such as `instance` or `Time`, like a SQL join.
- **Reduce**: turn each series into a row with calculations (last, mean, max) across the time range; perfect for "per instance summary" tables.
- **Organize fields by name**: rename, reorder and hide columns.
- **Filter data by values**, **Filter fields by name**: drop rows or columns.
- **Add field from calculation**: compute a new column, for example a ratio of two columns or a row total.
- **Group by**, **Sort by**, **Labels to fields** and **Convert field type**.

Transformations run in the **browser** on already-fetched data, so they can't reduce how much data the query returns. When a calculation can be done in the query itself (PromQL division, aggregation), do it there: it's faster and works the same in alerting. Use transformations for presentation and for combining data from different data sources.
takeaways: Transformations reshape results in the browser, in order
Merge, Join by field, Reduce and Organize fields cover most tables
Prefer doing maths in the query when possible
pitfalls: Fetching huge raw data and filtering with transformations instead of filtering in the query.

quiz.q: You want one table row per instance with columns from two queries. Which transformation combines them?
quiz.explain: Merge combines several query results into one frame by their common fields.

concepts.name: Rows, repeating panels and library panels
concepts.summary: Arrange panels on the 24-column grid, group them in collapsible rows, repeat panels or rows per variable value, and reuse library panels.
concepts.why: One well-laid-out, repeating dashboard replaces dozens of copies that drift apart.
concepts.body:
A dashboard is a **grid 24 columns wide**; each panel has a position and size (`gridPos` with `x`, `y`, `w`, `h` in the JSON model) and you drag and resize in edit mode. Put the most important summary panels at the top, details below, and keep panel heights consistent in a row so the eye can scan.

**Rows** are horizontal dividers that group panels and can be **collapsed**; collapsed rows don't run their queries until expanded, which makes big dashboards load fast. Row titles can use variables (`$job overview`).

**Repeat** creates copies per value of a multi-value variable:

- **Repeat panel** by `$instance`, horizontally with a maximum per row, or vertically. Each copy gets the variable bound to one value, so its query `up{instance="$instance"}` is per copy.
- **Repeat row** by `$cluster` repeats a whole row of panels, which is how per-environment or per-region sections are built.

Repeats are rendered only for the currently selected values; choosing All with fifty instances creates fifty panels and fifty queries, so give such variables a sensible default.

**Library panels** (Dashboards, Library panels) are panels stored once and linked into many dashboards. Edit the library panel and every dashboard using it updates; **Unlink** turns a linked copy back into a normal panel. They are ideal for a standard "service header" row or a legal-text panel that must be identical everywhere, and they carry their own permissions through folders.

Grafana 12 introduces new **dynamic layouts** (auto grid, tabs, conditional rendering) behind the dashboard v2 schema; the grid above remains the default.
concepts.code:
{
  "panels": [
    {"type": "row", "title": "$cluster", "collapsed": false,
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 24, "h": 1},
     "repeat": "cluster"},
    {"type": "stat", "title": "Up: $instance",
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 1, "w": 4, "h": 3},
     "repeat": "instance", "repeatDirection": "h", "maxPerRow": 6,
     "targets": [{"refId": "A", "instant": true,
                  "expr": "up{cluster=\"$cluster\", instance=\"$instance\"}"}]},
    {"type": "timeseries", "title": "Latency",
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 4, "w": 24, "h": 8},
     "libraryPanel": {"uid": "svc-latency", "name": "Service latency"}}
  ]
}
takeaways: 24-column grid; rows group and collapse panels and skip their queries while collapsed
Repeat panels or rows per selected value of a multi-value variable
Library panels are edited once and update everywhere they are linked
pitfalls: Repeating a panel by a variable whose All value expands to hundreds of items.

quiz.q: You need the same "service health" panel on 20 dashboards and want one place to change it. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Library panels are stored once and linked into many dashboards; edits propagate to all of them.

concepts.name: Annotations, dashboard links and data links
concepts.summary: Mark events with manual and query-driven annotations, link dashboards with variables and time range preserved, and make values clickable with data links.
concepts.why: Deploy markers and drill-down links are what turn a set of dashboards into a navigable system.
concepts.body:
**Annotations** are vertical markers (or shaded regions) drawn on time-based panels. The built-in **Annotations & Alerts** query shows annotations stored in Grafana's own database: those you add by hand (Ctrl/Cmd-click a graph, or drag to mark a region, with text and tags) and state changes of alert rules linked to the dashboard. Under **Settings, Annotations** you add **query** annotations from any data source: a Prometheus expression such as a restart counter, a Loki query for lines containing "deploy", or Grafana's own annotations filtered by tag, so a deploy pipeline can POST `{"tags": ["deploy","api"], "text": "v2.3.1"}` to `/api/annotations` and every dashboard with that tag filter shows it. Annotation queries run on every refresh, so keep them cheap.

**Dashboard links** (Settings, Links) appear at the top: a link to a URL, to a specific dashboard, or a drop-down of all dashboards with certain **tags**. Tick **Include current time range** and **Include current template variable values** so the target opens on the same service and window. **Panel links** do the same in a panel's menu.

**Data links** are attached to values: clicking a point, bar, table cell or stat opens a URL built from the data. Variables available include `${__value.raw}`, `${__value.time}`, `${__field.labels.instance}`, `${__series.name}`, `${__data.fields.pod}`, `${__url_time_range}` and `${__from}`/`${__to}`, plus dashboard variables. A link to another dashboard looks like `/d/pods?var-pod=${__field.labels.pod}&${__url_time_range}`; a link to Explore can carry a prepared query. **Correlations** (administration) define such links centrally, from one data source's results to a query in another.
concepts.code:
# Query annotation (Prometheus): process restarts, title/text from labels
changes(process_start_time_seconds{job="api"}[2m]) > 0
# Title: restart  Text: {{instance}}  Tags: restart

# Deploy markers posted by CI (shown by a Grafana annotation query filtered on tag "deploy")
# curl -X POST https://grafana.example.com/api/annotations \
#   -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
#   -d '{"tags":["deploy","api"],"text":"api v2.3.1"}'

# Data link on a "requests by pod" panel -> pod dashboard, same time range
# Title: Open pod
# URL:   /d/pods/pod-detail?var-namespace=$namespace&var-pod=${__field.labels.pod}&${__url_time_range}

# Data link to Explore with Loki logs for the clicked series
# URL:   /explore?left={"datasource":"loki","queries":[{"expr":"{pod=\"${__field.labels.pod}\"}"}],"range":{"from":"${__from}","to":"${__to}"}}
takeaways: Annotations come from Grafana's DB (manual, alerts, API) or from data source queries
Dashboard links can carry the time range and variable values to the target
Data links build URLs from the clicked value's labels and time
pitfalls: A data link to another dashboard without ${__url_time_range}, so it opens on the default range and the spike is gone.

quiz.q: A CI pipeline should mark each deployment on every dashboard of the service. What is the simplest way?
options: Add a text panel listing deployments
POST a tagged annotation to the Grafana API and add a tag-filtered annotation query to the dashboards
Create an alert rule per deployment
quiz.explain: Grafana-stored annotations filtered by tag appear on any dashboard that queries those tags.

concepts.name: Dashboard JSON model, export and versions
concepts.summary: Read the dashboard JSON model (uid, panels, templating, schemaVersion), export and import portable JSON, and compare and restore versions.
concepts.why: Everything the UI does ends up in this JSON; reading it is the step from clicking dashboards to reviewing, generating and versioning them.
concepts.body:
Every dashboard is one JSON document, visible under **Edit, Settings, JSON Model**. The important fields:

- `uid`: the stable identifier used in URLs (`/d/<uid>/<slug>`) and links. `id` is a per-instance database number; it is ignored on import and should be `null` in files.
- `title`, `tags`, `timezone`, `time` (default range), `refresh`, `graphTooltip`.
- `templating.list`: the variables, each with `query`, `datasource`, `multi`, `includeAll`, `current`.
- `annotations.list` and `links`.
- `panels[]`: each with `type`, `gridPos`, `datasource` (`{"type": "prometheus", "uid": "prom-main"}`), `targets` (queries), `fieldConfig.defaults` and `overrides`, `options`, and `transformations`. Rows are panels of type `row` holding collapsed panels.
- `schemaVersion` and `version`: Grafana migrates old schemas on load; the version number increases with every save.

**Export** (Share, Export) offers the raw model or **Export for sharing externally**, which replaces concrete data source UIDs with placeholders like `${DS_PROMETHEUS}` listed under `__inputs`. On **Import** (Dashboards, New, Import) the user maps each input to a local data source, and that is how dashboards from grafana.com/dashboards, where every published dashboard has a numeric id, work across installations.

**Versions** (Settings, Versions) lists every save with author and message, lets you **compare** two versions as a JSON diff, and **restore** an older one, which creates a new version rather than rewriting history. Provisioned dashboards keep their history too but are overwritten from the file.

Grafana 12 adds a **v2 schema** and a Kubernetes-style dashboards API (`dashboard.grafana.app`), used by the new layouts and Git Sync; the classic model above remains supported and is still what most tooling emits.
concepts.code:
{
  "uid": "api-overview",
  "id": null,
  "title": "API overview",
  "tags": ["api", "service"],
  "timezone": "browser",
  "schemaVersion": 41,
  "version": 17,
  "time": {"from": "now-6h", "to": "now"},
  "refresh": "1m",
  "graphTooltip": 1,
  "templating": {"list": [{
    "name": "job", "type": "query", "query": "label_values(up, job)",
    "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "${DS_PROMETHEUS}"},
    "refresh": 2, "multi": false, "includeAll": false}]},
  "__inputs": [{"name": "DS_PROMETHEUS", "type": "datasource",
                "pluginId": "prometheus", "label": "Prometheus"}],
  "panels": [{
    "id": 1, "type": "timeseries", "title": "Requests",
    "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 12, "h": 8},
    "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "${DS_PROMETHEUS}"},
    "targets": [{"refId": "A", "expr": "sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"$job\"}[$__rate_interval]))"}],
    "fieldConfig": {"defaults": {"unit": "reqps"}, "overrides": []},
    "options": {}
  }]
}
takeaways: uid is stable and used in URLs; id is instance-local and should be null in files
Export for sharing externally replaces data sources with ${DS_*} inputs mapped on import
Versions can be compared as a JSON diff and restored
pitfalls: Copying a dashboard JSON between instances with concrete data source uids that don't exist there, so every panel shows "datasource not found".

quiz.q: What does "Export for sharing externally" change in the JSON?
options: It replaces data source references with ${DS_...} inputs that are mapped on import
It converts the dashboard to the v2 schema
quiz.explain: The __inputs block lets the importer bind each placeholder to a local data source.

concepts.name: Dashboard design: RED, USE, golden signals
concepts.summary: Structure dashboards around RED, USE and the four golden signals, build a drill-down hierarchy, and apply layout conventions that work in incidents.
concepts.why: Most dashboards fail not for lack of data but because nobody can answer "is it broken, and where?" from them in thirty seconds.
concepts.body:
Good dashboards answer a question for an audience. Three well-known frameworks tell you which panels belong on them:

- **RED** for request-driven services: **Rate** (requests per second), **Errors** (failed requests per second or error ratio), **Duration** (latency distribution, p50/p95/p99 or a heatmap). One row of RED per service, split by endpoint below.
- **USE** for resources (CPU, memory, disk, network, queues): **Utilization** (how busy), **Saturation** (how much queued or over capacity), **Errors**.
- The **four golden signals** from Google's SRE book: latency, traffic, errors and saturation, which is RED plus saturation.

Organise dashboards as a **hierarchy** with links between the levels: an overview with one stat row per service (traffic, error ratio, p95, with thresholds), a per-service dashboard with the RED rows and dependencies, and detail dashboards per instance, pod or database. Data links and tag-based dashboard links let you drill down without losing the time range.

Layout conventions:

- Top-left is the most important thing; summary stats first, time series below, tables and logs last.
- Same unit, colour and Y-axis scale for the same quantity everywhere; green/yellow/red thresholds only where they mean something, taken from your SLOs.
- Short titles, a **description** on every non-obvious panel (shown on hover), and legend names that fit.
- One dashboard per audience and purpose; a wall screen, an on-call view and a capacity planning dashboard are different dashboards.

Finally, use **variables** for environment and service so you maintain one dashboard, and keep it in version control.
concepts.code:
# Service overview row (per $service), RED
# Rate (req/s)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Error ratio (percentunit, thresholds at SLO: orange 0.1%, red 1%)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service", status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Duration p95 (seconds)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Resource row, USE (CPU)
# Utilization
1 - avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Saturation (run queue per core)
node_load1{instance=~"$instance"} / count without (cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle", instance=~"$instance"})
takeaways: RED for services, USE for resources, golden signals = RED + saturation
Build a drill-down hierarchy: overview, service, instance, linked with time range preserved
Consistent units, colours and thresholds tied to SLOs
pitfalls: A dashboard that is a dump of every metric the exporter has, instead of the handful that answer "is it healthy?".

quiz.q: Which three panels make up a RED row for an HTTP service?
options: Request rate, error rate, request duration
quiz.explain: RED stands for Rate, Errors and Duration; USE is the resource-oriented counterpart.

concepts.name: SQL data sources and macros
concepts.summary: Chart data from PostgreSQL or MySQL with time-series queries, Grafana's time macros and table formats.
concepts.why: Business metrics often live in relational databases, and Grafana can chart them next to system metrics.
concepts.body:
Grafana ships PostgreSQL, MySQL and Microsoft SQL Server data sources. Configure them with a **read-only database user**: dashboard users can run any query the data source allows.

A query can be formatted as a **table** or a **time series**. For time series, return a column named `time` (a timestamp or epoch), one or more numeric value columns, and optionally a text column used as the series name (`metric`). Sort by time.

**Macros** insert the dashboard's time range and interval into SQL:

- `$__timeFilter(created_at)` becomes a `BETWEEN` condition for the selected range, so the database can use an index on that column.
- `$__timeGroupAlias(created_at, $__interval)` buckets timestamps into intervals and aliases the column as `time`.
- `$__timeFrom()` and `$__timeTo()` give the range bounds; `$__unixEpochFilter()` handles integer timestamps.

Dashboard variables work in SQL too, including query variables like `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers`. Multi-value variables are rendered as a comma-separated quoted list for `IN ($country)`.

Keep queries cheap: always filter with `$__timeFilter`, aggregate in SQL, and point Grafana at a replica rather than the primary production database.
concepts.code:
-- Orders per interval by country, as a time series panel
SELECT
  $__timeGroupAlias(created_at, $__interval),
  country AS metric,
  count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE $__timeFilter(created_at)
  AND country IN ($country)          -- multi-value variable
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;

-- Expands roughly to (PostgreSQL):
-- SELECT floor(extract(epoch from created_at)/60)*60 AS "time", ...
-- WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-10-17T06:00:00Z' AND '2026-10-17T12:00:00Z'
--   AND country IN ('DE','FR')
takeaways: Time series queries return time, value columns and an optional metric column
$__timeFilter and $__timeGroupAlias inject the dashboard range and interval
Use a read-only user and preferably a replica
pitfalls: Forgetting $__timeFilter, so every refresh scans the whole table.

quiz.q: What does $__timeFilter(created_at) do?
options: Adds a condition restricting created_at to the dashboard's time range
quiz.explain: It expands to a range condition using the selected from and to times.

concepts.name: Loki and LogQL basics
concepts.summary: Query logs in Loki: stream selectors, line filters, json and logfmt parsers, label filters, line_format, and metric queries that turn logs into graphs.
concepts.why: Loki is the logs half of the Grafana stack, and LogQL is how you go from "something is wrong" to the lines that say what.
concepts.body:
**Loki** stores log lines in **streams** identified by a small set of labels (`app`, `namespace`, `pod`, `level`), indexing only those labels, not the text. That is why it is cheap and why high-cardinality values such as user or request IDs must stay inside the line (or in structured metadata), not become labels.

A **LogQL** query is a pipeline:

- **Stream selector**: `{app="api", env="prod"}`, with `=`, `!=`, `=~`, `!~` like PromQL. At least one non-empty matcher is required.
- **Line filters**: `|= "error"` contains, `!= "healthz"` does not contain, `|~ "timeout|refused"` regex, `!~` not regex. They are fast; put them first.
- **Parsers** extract fields from the line: `| json`, `| logfmt`, `| pattern "<ip> - <_> <method> <path>"`, `| regexp "..."`.
- **Label filters** on extracted fields: `| status >= 500`, `| duration > 2s`, `| method="POST"`.
- **Formatting**: `| line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.duration}}"` rewrites the line, `| label_format` renames labels, `| drop`/`| keep` trim fields.

**Metric queries** wrap a log query in a range function and aggregate like PromQL: `count_over_time({app="api"} |= "error" [5m])` counts lines, `rate(...)` per second, `bytes_rate` bytes per second, and `sum by (status) (...)` groups. With `| unwrap duration` you can compute `quantile_over_time(0.95, ... [5m]) by (path)` from values in the logs. These queries draw graphs and can feed alert rules.

In Explore, the **log volume** histogram above the lines shows counts by level, the **Logs** app (Logs Drilldown) offers a query-less browsing view, and clicking a label value adds it to the selector.
concepts.code:
# Streams of the API in prod, lines containing "error" but not health checks
{app="api", env="prod"} |= "error" != "/healthz"

# Parse JSON logs, keep slow 5xx responses, reshape the line
{app="api"} | json | status >= 500 | duration > 1s
  | line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.status}} {{.duration}}"

# logfmt lines (level=error msg="..." ) from one namespace
{namespace="payments"} | logfmt | level="error"

# Metric query: error lines per second, by app
sum by (app) (rate({env="prod"} |= "error" [5m]))

# p95 request duration computed from log fields, by path
quantile_over_time(0.95,
  {app="api"} | json | unwrap duration_ms [5m]) by (path)
takeaways: Stream selector first, then line filters, then parsers and label filters
Only labels are indexed; keep high-cardinality values in the line
count_over_time, rate and unwrap turn logs into metrics and alerts
pitfalls: Putting `| json` before a line filter, so Loki parses every line instead of discarding most of them cheaply first.

quiz.q: Which query counts error lines per second for each app in prod?
quiz.explain: rate over a log selection in a range window, aggregated by app, is the LogQL metric-query form.

concepts.name: Tempo traces and TraceQL
concepts.summary: Find and read distributed traces in Tempo: spans and attributes, TraceQL filters and aggregates, the trace waterfall view, and the service graph.
concepts.why: When a request is slow across five services, a trace shows which hop took the time; metrics and logs can't.
concepts.body:
A **trace** records one request's path through a system as a tree of **spans**: each span has a name, a start time and duration, a parent, and **attributes** such as `http.status_code` or `db.statement`, plus **resource** attributes identifying the service (`service.name`). Applications emit them with OpenTelemetry, and **Tempo** stores them cheaply in object storage, indexed by trace ID and, with its columnar format, searchable by attributes.

In Explore the Tempo data source offers:

- **TraceQL** queries. `{ resource.service.name = "api" && span.http.status_code >= 500 }` selects traces containing a matching span; `duration > 2s` filters by span duration, `traceDuration` by the whole trace. Pipelines aggregate: `{ ... } | count() > 3` for traces with more than three such spans, `| avg(duration) > 1s`. Structural operators find parent/child relations, for example `{ span.http.route = "/checkout" } >> { resource.service.name = "payments" }`. The **Search** tab builds these without typing.
- **TraceQL metrics** (`| rate()`, `| quantile_over_time(duration, .95)` by attributes) chart traces like metrics, when the Tempo metrics-generator is enabled.
- Paste a **trace ID** to open it directly.

The **trace view** is a waterfall: spans nested by parent, bars scaled to duration, with a minimap to zoom, span details (attributes, events, logs) on click, and a critical-path highlight. Long bars with nothing under them mean time spent inside that service; many short sibling bars mean chatty calls that could be batched.

Tempo's metrics-generator can also derive **span metrics** and a **service graph** (nodes per service, edges with request rate, error ratio and latency), shown in the Node graph visualization, so RED dashboards exist even for services that have no metrics instrumentation.
takeaways: Traces are trees of spans with attributes; resource.* identifies the service, span.* the operation
TraceQL filters spans with { } and aggregates with | count(), | avg()
The waterfall view shows where time goes; the service graph gives RED per service
pitfalls: Searching without any service or attribute filter over a long range, which scans most of the trace store.

quiz.q: What does { resource.service.name = "api" && duration > 2s } return?
options: Traces whose total duration is over 2s
Traces containing a span of the api service that lasted over 2s
Only the slow spans, without their trace
An error, duration needs a unit in milliseconds
quiz.explain: A { } block matches spans; a trace is returned when it contains a span satisfying all conditions.

concepts.name: Correlating metrics, logs and traces
concepts.summary: Jump from a latency spike to the trace behind it and from a span to its logs with exemplars, derived fields, trace-to-logs links and split view.
concepts.why: During an incident you move from a spike in a graph to the log lines and the slow trace behind it; the correlation settings are what make that one click instead of copy-paste.
concepts.body:
Metrics, logs and traces each answer a different question; **correlations** are the configured links that let you move between them in Explore and on dashboards without retyping identifiers. They all rely on **shared labels** (`service`, `namespace`, `pod`, `cluster`) being named the same across Prometheus, Loki and Tempo, and on applications writing the **trace ID** into their logs.

The main links, configured on the data sources:

- **Exemplars** (Prometheus data source, Exemplars section): Prometheus can store a trace ID alongside histogram samples when started with exemplar storage. Enable exemplars on a panel's query and they show as diamonds on latency graphs; the internal link maps the `trace_id` label to the Tempo data source, so one click opens the exact slow request.
- **Derived fields** (Loki data source): a regex such as `traceID=(\w+)` or a structured-metadata field becomes a link next to each log line, pointing to Tempo with the matched ID. Clicking a line's **Logs context** shows surrounding lines.
- **Trace to logs** (Tempo data source): a span's service and time range become a Loki query. Map tags (`service.name` to `app`), add a time shift before and after the span, and optionally filter by trace or span ID.
- **Trace to metrics**: query templates per span, for example the service's error ratio with `$__tags` substituted from span attributes. **Trace to profiles** does the same with Pyroscope.
- **Correlations** (Administration, Plugins and data): generic links from any result field of one data source to a query in another, with regex transformations.

The working pattern in Explore: open the RED graph, hover an exemplar, open the trace in **split view**, pick the slow span, jump to its logs. On dashboards, data links to Explore give the same path from a panel. When a hop fails, it is almost always a label mismatch or a missing trace ID in the logs.
concepts.code:
# Prometheus data source -> Exemplars
#   Internal link: Tempo       Label name: trace_id
# Panel query with exemplars enabled:
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Loki data source -> Derived fields
#   Name: TraceID   Regex: traceID=(\w+)   Internal link: Tempo   Query: ${__value.raw}
# Log line: level=error msg="timeout" traceID=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736

# Tempo data source -> Trace to logs
#   Data source: Loki   Tags: service.name -> app   Span start -1m / end +1m
# Generated for a span of service "api":
{app="api"} |= "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"

# Tempo -> Trace to metrics, query template using span tags
sum(rate(http_requests_total{$__tags, status=~"5.."}[5m]))
takeaways: Exemplars link graph points to traces; derived fields link log lines to traces
Trace to logs and trace to metrics turn a span into Loki and Prometheus queries by mapping tags
Shared label names and trace IDs in logs are what make the jumps work
pitfalls: Tempo's trace-to-logs tag mapping left at defaults, so the generated Loki query uses service.name as a label and returns nothing.

quiz.q: What is an exemplar?
options: A trace ID attached to a metric sample, linking a graph point to a trace
quiz.explain: Exemplars connect individual metric observations to the trace that produced them.

quiz.q: Clicking a Tempo span's logs button returns no lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The trace-to-logs tag mapping doesn't match the Loki label names, or the log lines lack the trace ID
Exemplars are disabled on the Prometheus data source
quiz.explain: The generated query is built from mapped span tags; wrong label names or missing IDs select nothing.

concepts.name: Grafana Alerting overview
concepts.summary: Create alert rules with queries, expressions and pending periods, and route notifications through contact points and notification policies.
concepts.why: Dashboards only help when someone is looking; alert rules turn them into notifications.
concepts.body:
Grafana Alerting has three main parts, found under **Alerting**:

- **Alert rules**: one or more queries, then **expressions** that reduce and compare them, for example query A, **Reduce** to the last value, **Threshold** above 0.05. Rules are evaluated by an **evaluation group** on an interval, and have a **pending period**: the condition must hold that long before the alert fires, just like Prometheus's `for`. Rules can carry labels and annotations such as summary and runbook URL, and can be linked to a dashboard panel.
- **Contact points**: where notifications go: email, Slack, PagerDuty, Microsoft Teams, webhooks and more, with templated messages.
- **Notification policies**: a tree that matches alert labels to contact points, with grouping, timing and nested policies, the same model as Prometheus Alertmanager. **Silences** and **mute timings** suppress notifications temporarily or on a schedule.

Grafana-managed rules can query **any** backend data source, including SQL databases, and combine several. For Prometheus or Mimir you can alternatively manage **data source-managed rules**, which are evaluated by the Prometheus ruler and routed by Alertmanager.

Each series returned by the query becomes its own alert instance, labelled by its labels, so one rule covers every instance. Configure **No data** and **Error** handling explicitly; the defaults decide whether a broken query pages you.
concepts.code:
# Grafana-managed alert rule (conceptual layout of the UI form)
# Query A (Prometheus):
sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# Expression B: Reduce   A  -> Last
# Expression C: Threshold B  -> Is above 0.05     (alert condition)
# Folder: Services  Evaluation group: api (every 1m)  Pending period: 5m
# Labels: severity=page team=api
# Annotations:
#   summary = Error ratio for {{ $labels.job }} is {{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }}
# Notification policy: team=api -> contact point "api-oncall" (PagerDuty)
# No data: Keep last state    Error: Alerting
takeaways: Rules = queries + Reduce/Threshold expressions + pending period
Contact points send; notification policies route by labels
Each returned series becomes a separate alert instance
pitfalls: Leaving No data handling at its default without thinking, so an exporter outage silently stops alerting or pages everyone.

quiz.q: How does a Grafana alert rule notify the right team?
options: Notification policies match the alert's labels to contact points
Each rule names an email address
quiz.explain: Routing is label-based through the notification policy tree.

concepts.name: Alert rule anatomy: queries and expressions
concepts.summary: Build a Grafana-managed rule step by step: queries, Reduce, Math and Threshold expressions, the condition, labels, templated annotations, pending period.
concepts.why: A rule is a small data pipeline; understanding each stage is what lets you debug "why did this fire?" and "why didn't it?".
concepts.body:
A **Grafana-managed alert rule** is built in the rule editor as a chain of **queries** and **expressions**, each with a letter (`A`, `B`, `C`), and exactly one of them is marked as the **alert condition**.

- **Queries** run against any backend data source, over a relative window such as last 5 minutes. Each series returned becomes a separate **alert instance**, labelled with the series labels, so one rule covers every job, pod or disk.
- **Reduce** turns each time series into a number: function Last, Mean, Min, Max, Sum, Count; mode Strict (NaN if any point is non-numeric), Replace non-numbers, or Drop non-numbers.
- **Math** evaluates an expression over earlier results: `$B > 0.05`, `$A / $C * 100`, `abs($A - $B)`. Series are matched by labels.
- **Threshold** compares with above, below, within range or outside range, and can define a **custom recovery threshold** (hysteresis) so an alert at 90% resolves only below 80%.
- **Classic condition** combines several queries into one instance, which loses the per-series labels; prefer the others.

The condition's result is boolean per instance: 1 fires. The **simplified** rule editor hides B and C behind "WHEN last() OF A IS ABOVE 0.05" and builds the same chain.

Then the rule gets a **folder** and **evaluation group** (which fixes the interval), a **pending period** such as 5m (the condition must stay true that long; 0 fires immediately) and in recent versions **keep firing for**, which holds a resolved alert for a while to avoid flapping notifications.

**Labels** (`severity=page`, `team=api`, templates allowed) drive routing. **Annotations** carry human text: `summary`, `description`, `runbook_url`, templated with `{{ $labels.job }}`, `{{ $values.B }}` or `{{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }}`. Link the rule to a **dashboard and panel** so notifications include a link, and use **Preview** to see instances before saving.
concepts.code:
# Query A (Prometheus, last 5m):
sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# Expression B: Reduce     input A, function Last, mode Strict
# Expression C: Threshold  input B, IS ABOVE 0.05,
#                          custom recovery threshold: below 0.02   <- alert condition

# Rule settings
# Folder: Services        Evaluation group: api-fast (every 1m)
# Pending period: 5m      Keep firing for: 2m
# Labels:      severity=page   team=api   service={{ $labels.job }}
# Annotations:
#   summary     = High error ratio for {{ $labels.job }}
#   description = {{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }} of requests failed over the last 5m
#   runbook_url = https://runbooks.example.com/api/error-ratio
# Dashboard: API overview   Panel: Error ratio
takeaways: Rule = queries + Reduce/Math/Threshold expressions; one is the alert condition
Every returned series becomes its own alert instance with its labels
Labels route, annotations explain; both can use {{ $labels }} and {{ $values }}
pitfalls: Using Classic condition out of habit and losing the per-instance labels the notification policy needs.

quiz.q: Query A returns 12 series, one per pod. How many alert instances can the rule produce?
options: Up to 12, one per pod, each with the pod's labels
None until a Classic condition is added
quiz.explain: Grafana evaluates the condition per series; each series is a separate labelled alert instance.

quiz.q: Which expression type lets an alert fire above 90% but resolve only below 80%?
options: Threshold with a custom recovery threshold
quiz.explain: The recovery threshold adds hysteresis so the instance doesn't flap around one value.

concepts.name: Contact points and notification policies
concepts.summary: Route alerts: contact point integrations and templates, the notification policy tree with matchers and grouping, timings, mute timings and silences.
concepts.why: Alerts are only as good as who receives them and when; routing decides whether a page is useful or noise.
concepts.body:
A **contact point** is a named destination with one or more **integrations**: email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Discord, Telegram, webhook, OnCall, and others. Each has its own settings and a **Test** button that sends a sample alert. The message content comes from **notification templates**, Go templates you can customise, for example a Slack title that lists `{{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}` and a body that loops over `.Alerts` with their annotations and silence links.

The **notification policy tree** decides which contact point gets which alerts. The **default policy** at the root catches everything; **child policies** add **label matchers** (`team = api`, `severity =~ "page|critical"`). Evaluation walks the tree depth-first and stops at the first matching policy, unless that policy sets **continue matching**, which lets an alert hit several siblings (a Slack channel and PagerDuty). Each policy can override:

- **Group by** labels (default `grafana_folder`, `alertname`): alerts with the same values are bundled into one notification.
- **Group wait** (30s): how long to collect alerts before the first notification of a new group.
- **Group interval** (5m): minimum time between updates for a changed group.
- **Repeat interval** (4h): how often an unchanged, still-firing group is re-sent.

**Mute timings** are schedules (weekends, nightly maintenance) attached to a policy; during them notifications are held, not dropped. **Silences** are ad hoc: label matchers plus a duration, created from a firing alert with one click, and they only stop notifications, the rule keeps evaluating and the alert shows as suppressed.

An alert rule can also name a contact point directly (**simplified routing**), bypassing the tree, which is handy for small teams. Both contact points and policies can be exported as YAML or Terraform and provisioned.
concepts.code:
# Notification policy tree (Alerting > Notification policies), exported form
apiVersion: 1
policies:
  - orgId: 1
    receiver: default-email            # root: catches everything else
    group_by: [grafana_folder, alertname]
    group_wait: 30s
    group_interval: 5m
    repeat_interval: 4h
    routes:
      - receiver: api-pagerduty
        object_matchers:
          - [team, =, api]
          - [severity, =, page]
        continue: true                 # also try the next sibling
      - receiver: api-slack
        object_matchers:
          - [team, =, api]
        mute_time_intervals: [weekends]
        repeat_interval: 24h
takeaways: Contact points send; policies match labels to contact points, first match wins unless continue is set
Group by, group wait, group interval and repeat interval control bundling and repetition
Mute timings are scheduled, silences are ad hoc; both only suppress notifications
pitfalls: A child policy with continue off placed above a more specific one, so the specific policy never receives anything.

quiz.q: An alert with team=api, severity=page should go to both PagerDuty and the team's Slack channel. What makes that possible?
options: A policy with continue matching enabled so sibling policies are also evaluated
A silence on the Slack policy
quiz.explain: Without continue, the first matching policy stops the walk through the tree.

concepts.name: Alert states, evaluation groups and history
concepts.summary: How evaluation groups schedule rules, the Normal, Pending, Alerting, Recovering, NoData and Error states, no-data handling and state history.
concepts.why: Knowing how an instance moves between states explains every "it fired late", "it never resolved" and "why did I get a DatasourceNoData page".
concepts.body:
Rules live in **evaluation groups** inside a folder. The group sets the **evaluation interval** (every 1m, 5m, ...), and all rules in it are evaluated on that schedule; a rule's pending period should be a multiple of it. Grafana runs the queries, computes the condition per instance and updates each instance's **state**:

- **Normal**: condition false.
- **Pending**: condition true, but not yet for the whole pending period.
- **Alerting** (firing): condition true for at least the pending period; a notification is sent to Alertmanager routing.
- **Recovering**: condition became false but **keep firing for** has not elapsed yet.
- **NoData**: the query returned nothing.
- **Error**: the query or expression failed.

A transition into Alerting sends the alert; a transition back to Normal sends a **resolved** notification. Alerts are re-sent at the policy's repeat interval while firing.

The rule's **No data** and **Error** handling settings decide what those situations map to: Alerting, Normal (OK), NoData/Error as their own states (which raise special `DatasourceNoData` and `DatasourceError` alerts with the rule's labels), or **Keep last state**. Which one is right depends on the rule: for a "disk full" rule, no data probably means the exporter died and should page; for a rarely non-zero metric, no data is Normal. Instances whose series disappear are resolved after a configurable number of missed evaluations (**missing series evaluations to resolve**), so stale pods don't fire forever.

**Rule health** (ok, error, nodata) is separate from instance state and shown in the rule list. The **state history** view (Alerting, History, or on the rule) shows every transition with the values that caused it; it can be stored as annotations or in Loki. Pausing a rule stops evaluation without deleting it. Grafana also exports `grafana_alerting_*` metrics for monitoring the alerting system itself.
concepts.code:
# Timeline of one instance, evaluation every 1m, pending period 5m, keep firing 2m
# t=0   value 0.02  Normal
# t=1   value 0.08  Pending     (condition true, 0m of 5m)
# t=5   value 0.07  Pending     (4m)
# t=6   value 0.09  Alerting    -> notification sent
# t=9   query fails Error       -> depends on Error handling (Alerting / Error / OK / Keep last)
# t=10  value 0.01  Recovering  (keep firing for 2m)
# t=12  value 0.01  Normal      -> resolved notification

# Provisioned rule excerpt showing the handling settings
#   for: 5m
#   keep_firing_for: 2m
#   noDataState: NoData        # Alerting | NoData | OK | KeepLast
#   execErrState: Error        # Alerting | Error  | OK | KeepLast
takeaways: Normal, Pending, Alerting, Recovering, NoData, Error per instance; health per rule
Notifications go out on entering Alerting and on resolve, then every repeat interval
Choose No data and Error handling per rule; missing series resolve after a few evaluations
pitfalls: Setting a 5m pending period on a group evaluated every 10m, so the alert needs two evaluations and fires after up to 20 minutes.

quiz.q: A rule has No data handling set to NoData. The exporter stops. What happens?
options: A DatasourceNoData alert with the rule's labels is raised and routed
quiz.explain: The NoData state creates a special alert so the routing can notify someone that the data is missing.

concepts.name: Provisioning and dashboards as code
concepts.summary: Define data sources and dashboards in files, understand the dashboard JSON model, and manage Grafana from Git with provisioning, Terraform or Git Sync.
concepts.why: Clicked-together dashboards get lost and drift between environments; code makes them reviewable and reproducible.
concepts.body:
**File provisioning** configures Grafana at startup from YAML files in `/etc/grafana/provisioning/`:

- `datasources/*.yaml`: data sources with name, type, URL, a fixed `uid` and secure settings taken from environment variables.
- `dashboards/*.yaml`: **providers** that load dashboard JSON files from a directory into a folder, and optionally reload on change (`updateIntervalSeconds`).
- `alerting/*.yaml`: alert rules, contact points and policies.

Every dashboard is a **JSON model** (Dashboard settings, JSON Model, or **Export**). Key fields: a stable `uid` (used in URLs and links), `title`, `panels`, `templating` (variables), `time` and `schemaVersion`. Use **data source UIDs or variables** in panels, not environment-specific names, so the same JSON works in staging and production.

Other ways to manage Grafana as code:

- The **HTTP API** with a **service account** token, used by scripts and CI.
- The **Terraform provider** for dashboards, folders, data sources, alerting and permissions.
- SDKs that generate dashboard JSON from code (the Grafana Foundation SDK, Jsonnet with Grafonnet).
- **Git Sync**, generally available since Grafana 13, connects dashboards and folders to a GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or plain Git repository, so UI edits become commits or pull requests.

Provisioned dashboards can't be saved over in the UI by default; changes go through the files.
concepts.code:
# /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prom-main                     # stable id referenced by dashboards
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
    jsonData:
      timeInterval: 15s                # = Prometheus scrape interval
---
# /etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/default.yaml
apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: services
    folder: Services
    type: file
    allowUiUpdates: false
    updateIntervalSeconds: 30
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards  # *.json dashboard models
takeaways: Provisioning YAML defines data sources, dashboards and alerting at startup
Dashboards are JSON models; give them and data sources stable UIDs
Automate with the API, Terraform or Git-based workflows
pitfalls: Hard-coding data source names in dashboard JSON so it breaks in other environments.

quiz.q: Why give a provisioned data source a fixed uid?
options: Dashboards reference data sources by uid, so it must be the same everywhere
quiz.explain: A stable uid keeps dashboard references valid across environments and re-provisioning.

concepts.name: Grafana as code: grafana.ini and Terraform
concepts.summary: Configure the server with grafana.ini and GF_ variables, and manage folders, dashboards, data sources and alerting with the Terraform provider.
concepts.why: Reproducible Grafana means every environment can be rebuilt from a repo, and every change is a reviewed diff.
concepts.body:
**Server configuration** is `grafana.ini` (defaults in `defaults.ini`, overrides in `custom.ini` or `/etc/grafana/grafana.ini`). Sections you touch most: `[server]` (`root_url`, `domain`, `serve_from_sub_path`), `[database]`, `[security]` (`admin_password`, `secret_key`, cookie flags), `[auth.*]` providers, `[users]` (`default_theme`, `viewers_can_edit`), `[dashboards]` (`min_refresh_interval`), `[unified_alerting]`, `[smtp]`, `[log]`. Any key maps to `GF_<SECTION>_<KEY>` in upper case, so containers are configured with environment variables, and values can reference `$__env{NAME}` or `$__file{/run/secrets/x}` to keep secrets out of the file. The effective configuration is visible under **Administration, General, Settings**.

For the objects inside Grafana, file provisioning works for data sources and dashboards, but the **Terraform provider** (`grafana/grafana`) covers everything with state and diffs:

- `grafana_folder`, `grafana_dashboard` (with `config_json = file("...")`), `grafana_library_panel`.
- `grafana_data_source` with `json_data_encoded` and `secure_json_data_encoded`.
- `grafana_contact_point`, `grafana_notification_policy`, `grafana_mute_timing`, `grafana_rule_group`.
- `grafana_team`, `grafana_user`, `grafana_folder_permission`, `grafana_service_account` and its tokens.

Authenticate the provider with a **service account token** of a dedicated admin account. The UI helps you bootstrap: alert rules, contact points and policies have **Export** buttons that emit YAML, JSON or HCL; dashboards export JSON that you commit next to the Terraform.

The same resources can be driven by the HTTP API from scripts, by **Grizzly** (a CLI that applies Grafana resources from Jsonnet or YAML), or by **Git Sync**, where Grafana itself reads dashboards from a repository and turns UI edits into pull requests. Whatever the tool, the rule is the same: the repo is the source of truth and the UI is read-only for managed objects.
takeaways: grafana.ini keys map to GF_SECTION_KEY environment variables; use $__env and $__file for secrets
The Terraform provider manages folders, dashboards, data sources, alerting and permissions with diffs
Export buttons in the UI give you the YAML/HCL to start from
pitfalls: Editing a Terraform-managed dashboard in the UI; the next apply reverts it and the change is lost.

quiz.q: Which environment variable sets [server] root_url in a container?
quiz.explain: The pattern is GF_<SECTION>_<KEY> with section and key in upper case.

concepts.name: Grafana on Kubernetes with Helm
concepts.summary: Deploy Grafana with the official Helm chart: admin secret, persistence, provisioned data sources, dashboards from ConfigMaps, kube-prometheus-stack.
concepts.why: Most production Grafanas run in Kubernetes, and the chart's sidecar pattern is how teams ship dashboards with their applications.
concepts.body:
The **grafana/grafana Helm chart** (repository `https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts`) deploys a Deployment, Service, optional Ingress and a PersistentVolumeClaim. The values you set first:

- **Admin credentials**: `admin.existingSecret` pointing at a Secret with `admin-user` and `admin-password`, rather than `adminPassword` in plain values.
- **Persistence**: `persistence.enabled: true` keeps the SQLite database and plugins across restarts; for more than one replica use an external PostgreSQL/MySQL via `grafana.ini` values instead, since SQLite can't be shared.
- **grafana.ini** as a YAML map, rendered to the config file; `env` and `envFromSecret` for `GF_` variables.
- **datasources**: a provisioning file inline in values (`datasources.yaml`), typically pointing at the in-cluster Prometheus Service URL.
- **dashboardProviders** plus `dashboards` (from grafana.com ids or local JSON) for a static set.
